terms.plain: A short-period change scaled up as though it continued for a whole year. It makes monthly and quarterly figures look bigger, in both directions.
terms.formal: The rate of change over a sub-annual period compounded to its yearly equivalent.

terms.plain: The parts of a budget that cushion the cycle without anyone deciding anything — unemployment benefits rise and tax receipts fall in a downturn. Why deficits widen in recessions with no new policy.
terms.formal: Elements of government revenue and expenditure that vary counter-cyclically with output by construction, dampening the cycle without discretionary action.

terms.plain: When an annual inflation rate jumps or drops only because the month a year ago was unusual. It is arithmetic, not news, and it is predictable in advance.
terms.formal: The contribution to a year-on-year rate arising from the level of the comparison period rather than from current price changes.

terms.plain: One hundredth of a percentage point. 100 basis points is 1%. Used because saying "the yield rose 0.08 percentage points" is clumsy and easy to mishear.
terms.formal: A unit equal to 1/100th of one percent (0.0001), used to express changes in interest rates, yields and fees precisely.

terms.plain: The repeated pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity around trend. Irregular in length — post-war expansions have run from one year to more than ten.
terms.formal: Recurrent fluctuations in aggregate output, employment and income around a long-run trend, conventionally divided into expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

terms.plain: Borrowing in a low-rate currency to invest in a high-rate one without hedging. Earns the rate gap for long stretches and gives years of it back in a fortnight.
terms.formal: A position funded in a low-yielding currency and invested in a higher-yielding one with the exchange rate left unhedged, earning the differential and bearing depreciation risk.

terms.plain: The institution that sets a country's short-term interest rate and is usually charged with keeping inflation stable.
terms.formal: The public authority responsible for monetary policy, currency issuance and typically financial stability, operating under a legislated mandate.

terms.plain: The rule tying the forward exchange rate to the two currencies' interest rates, because otherwise there would be free money on the table. It is why hedging a foreign yield gives you back your own rate.
terms.formal: The no-arbitrage condition equating the forward premium or discount to the interest rate differential between two currencies.

terms.plain: The cost of a fixed basket of what households buy, weighted by how much they spend on each item. The usual headline inflation measure, and an average nobody experiences exactly.
terms.formal: A weighted index of consumer goods and services prices, with weights derived from household expenditure surveys and periodically rebased.

terms.plain: Falling prices. It sounds like good news and generally is not: debts get heavier in real terms and buyers postpone spending because things will be cheaper later.
terms.formal: A sustained decrease in the aggregate price level, raising the real burden of nominal debt and creating incentives to defer consumption.

terms.plain: The price of one currency in another. Always write down which currency is on top before doing any arithmetic — inverted quotes cause more errors than bad economics.
terms.formal: The rate at which one currency may be exchanged for another, quoted as units of a quote currency per unit of a base currency.

terms.plain: The very short-term US interest rate that the Federal Reserve targets. It anchors the short end of the yield curve, so almost every other US rate takes its cue from it.
terms.formal: The rate at which US depository institutions lend reserve balances to each other overnight, targeted by the Federal Reserve as its principal policy instrument.

terms.plain: Government taxation and spending. Where monetary policy changes the price of money, this adds or subtracts demand directly.
terms.formal: The use of government expenditure and revenue measures to influence aggregate demand, output and the distribution of income.

terms.plain: When investors rush into the safest, most liquid assets and abandon everything else. It widens exactly the spreads that relative value strategies are short.
terms.formal: A market episode in which demand shifts sharply toward the most liquid and creditworthy instruments, raising liquidity premia and widening spreads between otherwise similar securities.

terms.plain: The exchange rate agreed today for swapping currency on a future date. Set by the two countries' interest rates, not by anyone's forecast.
terms.formal: The contractually agreed rate for a currency exchange at a specified future date, determined by covered interest parity from spot and the interest rate differential.

terms.plain: The exchange rate for swapping currency now rather than at a future date.
terms.formal: The rate for immediate settlement of a currency exchange, conventionally two business days forward.

terms.plain: The total value of everything a country produces in a period. The standard measure of the size of an economy, and a flow rather than a stock of wealth.
terms.formal: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a period, measurable equivalently by production, expenditure or income.

terms.plain: The price index used to turn nominal GDP into real GDP. Broader than a consumer price index, because it covers everything the economy produces rather than what households buy.
terms.formal: The ratio of nominal to real GDP expressed as an index; an economy-wide price measure whose weights shift with the composition of output.

terms.plain: A sustained rise in the general level of prices, so that a unit of currency buys less than it did. Not one price rising — the whole level.
terms.formal: A sustained increase in the aggregate price level, measured as the change in a price index over a period.

terms.plain: Data that moves after the economy has turned — default rates, how long people stay unemployed. It confirms a turn; it never anticipates one.
terms.formal: A series that changes direction after aggregate activity has turned, useful for confirmation rather than for timing.

terms.plain: Data that moves before the economy does — new orders, building permits, the yield curve. Noisier than the rest, and the only kind with any forecasting value.
terms.formal: A series that historically changes direction in advance of aggregate activity, typically because it records decisions rather than outcomes.

terms.plain: What a central bank does to influence borrowing costs and the amount of money circulating — mainly by moving its policy interest rate up or down.
terms.formal: Central bank actions affecting the money supply and the level of short-term interest rates in pursuit of statutory objectives, typically price stability and employment.

terms.plain: GDP at current prices, which mixes producing more with charging more. Growth of 5% here can be 2% more output and 3% higher prices.
terms.formal: Gross domestic product measured at prevailing prices, incorporating both volume and price changes.

terms.plain: How far actual output sits above or below what the economy can sustainably produce. Negative means spare capacity; positive means it is running hot. This, not the growth rate, is what central banks respond to.
terms.formal: The difference between actual and potential output expressed as a percentage of potential; the principal cyclical input to monetary policy decisions.

terms.plain: The short-term interest rate a central bank sets. Everything else in fixed income is priced off it, which is how one overnight rate reaches a thirty-year mortgage.
terms.formal: The administered overnight or short-term rate at which a central bank lends to, or absorbs deposits from, the banking system.

terms.plain: What an economy could produce with its people and equipment fully but sustainably employed. Not a maximum, and never actually measured — it is estimated and revised.
terms.formal: The level of output consistent with sustainable utilisation of labour and capital without generating accelerating inflation; an unobservable quantity inferred from models.

terms.plain: The government's deficit or surplus before interest payments. It separates what the government is doing now from what it owes for what it did before.
terms.formal: Government revenue less non-interest expenditure; the fiscal measure used in debt sustainability analysis.

terms.plain: A survey asking firms whether conditions improved or worsened. Above 50 means more firms improving than not, so it measures how widespread a change is rather than how big.
terms.formal: A diffusion index built from business surveys where readings above 50 indicate more respondents reporting expansion than contraction; it measures breadth of change, not magnitude.

terms.plain: A central bank buying long-dated bonds with newly created reserves, to push long-term rates down when the short rate is already at zero and cannot be cut further.
terms.formal: Large-scale purchases of longer-maturity securities financed by reserve creation, intended to compress term premia when the policy rate is at its effective lower bound.

terms.plain: GDP with the effect of price changes stripped out, so it measures actual output rather than higher prices. This is the version that matters.
terms.formal: Gross domestic product measured at constant prices, deflated by a price index so that changes reflect volume rather than price.

terms.plain: The interest rate after stripping out expected inflation — what you actually gain in purchasing power rather than in dollars.
terms.formal: A nominal interest rate adjusted for expected inflation. Approximately nominal minus expected inflation; precisely, (1+nominal)/(1+inflation) - 1.

terms.plain: A meaningful, broad-based decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months — not just one weak quarter.
terms.formal: A significant, broadly diffused decline in economic activity persisting more than a few months, assessed across output, employment and income rather than by a single mechanical rule.
terms.reviewNote: I have deliberately avoided the popular 'two consecutive quarters of negative GDP' shorthand, which is not how the US dating body defines it. Verify the definition you want to standardise on.

terms.plain: Removing the regular calendar pattern from data so that one month can be compared with another. The adjustment factors come from history, so they misfire when behaviour changes.
terms.formal: Statistical removal of recurring intra-year variation from a time series, using factors estimated from historical patterns.

terms.plain: The extra yield lenders demand purely for tying their money up longer, over and above what they expect short-term rates to average. It is the price of putting up with uncertainty.
terms.formal: The component of a long-dated bond's yield in excess of the average expected future short-term rate over its life, compensating investors for interest rate and inflation uncertainty.

terms.plain: A line showing what interest rate you get for lending to the same borrower for different lengths of time — three months, two years, ten years, and so on.
terms.formal: A plot of the yields of a single issuer's debt against their maturities at a point in time, most commonly constructed from government securities.

terms.plain: When short-term interest rates are higher than long-term ones — the curve slopes downward instead of upward. It usually means the market expects rate cuts ahead.
terms.formal: A yield curve state in which yields on shorter maturities exceed those on longer maturities, typically reflecting expectations of future monetary easing.

terms.plain: The difference between two yields, quoted as one minus the other. For curve shape it is normally the long yield minus the short one, so a negative number means inversion.
terms.formal: The arithmetic difference between two yields, used to express curve slope (e.g. the 10-year minus the 2-year) or credit risk (a corporate yield minus a comparable government yield).

terms.plain: The annual return you would earn on a bond if you bought it at today's price and held it until it matured, collecting every payment along the way.
terms.formal: The single discount rate that equates the present value of a bond's remaining cash flows to its current market price, assuming all payments are made and coupons are reinvested at that same rate.
